author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Academic register: nominalisation, hedging and impersonal style: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: Complete with 3–4 words. ‘Unemployment rose sharply, which led to protests.’ → ‘___ in unemployment led to protests.’
questions.explanation: Nominalisation: adjective + noun replaces the clause.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is most appropriately hedged?
questions.explanation: *suggest* + *may* + *some* qualify the claim to match the evidence.
options: The findings suggest that exercise may improve concentration in some students.
The findings prove that exercise improves concentration.
Exercise definitely improves concentration in every student.
Exercise is very good for concentration.

questions.prompt: Choose the academic alternative to ‘look into the problem’.
questions.explanation: Formal single verbs replace phrasal verbs.

questions.prompt: ___ that urban growth will continue for several decades.
questions.explanation: Anticipatory *it* + passive is impersonal and formal.

questions.prompt: Which part is too informal for an essay? *Governments should cut down on spending, but they can't ignore the needs of kids.*
questions.explanation: Replace with *reduce*, *cannot*, *children*.

questions.prompt: Several studies have reported higher stress levels among night workers. ___ findings highlight the need for better scheduling.
questions.explanation: Summary reference: *These / Such findings*.

questions.prompt: Hedge the claim with *appear*: ‘Online learning reduces dropout rates.’ → ‘Online learning ___ dropout rates.’
questions.explanation: *appear to* + infinitive softens the claim.

questions.prompt: Which version is clearest and most academic?
questions.explanation: Balanced nominalisation with an active verb; option C overuses nouns.
options: The introduction of congestion charges reduced traffic by 20%.
When they introduced congestion charges, traffic went down by 20%.
The reduction of traffic by 20% was the result of the introduction of the charging of congestion.
Congestion charges got introduced and traffic was reduced 20%.

questions.prompt: Replace the informal phrase: ‘There are ___ (lots of) factors involved.’
questions.explanation: Academic quantifiers replace *lots of*.

questions.prompt: ‘___ is little evidence to support the claim that bilingual children fall behind.’
questions.explanation: *There is little evidence…* is an impersonal evaluative pattern.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Adjectives, adverbs and intensifiers: gradability, position and order: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: Choose the natural combination.
questions.explanation: *Exhausted* is an extreme adjective, so it takes *absolutely*.

questions.prompt: The new treatment is ___ effective in early cases.
questions.explanation: *Effective* is gradable and *highly effective* is a strong collocation.

questions.prompt: I ___ ever see my cousins now that they live abroad.
questions.explanation: *Hardly* = almost not.

questions.prompt: Correct the sentence: *She speaks very fluently Spanish.*
questions.explanation: Manner adverbs follow the object, not the verb.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct order.
questions.explanation: Opinion → age → material.

questions.prompt: "The film was quite brilliant." What does *quite* mean here?
questions.explanation: With a non-gradable adjective, *quite* means *completely*.

questions.prompt: The two theories are ___ different: they rest on opposite assumptions about human nature. (fundamental)
questions.explanation: *Fundamentally different* is a strong academic collocation.

questions.prompt: In a research report, which phrase is most appropriate? *Female respondents reported ___ higher levels of satisfaction.*
questions.explanation: *Markedly* is formal and precise.

questions.prompt: Rewrite so that the adverb comments on the whole sentence: *She did not explain the decision clearly.* Begin: *Clearly, ...*
questions.explanation: Front position turns *clearly* into a comment adverb (it is obvious that ...).
accepted: Clearly, she did not explain the decision.
Clearly, she didn't explain the decision.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses a post-positive adjective correctly?
questions.explanation: *The members present* = those who were there.
options: All the members present voted in favour.
All the present members voted in favour because they were here.
All the members presently voted in favour.
All present the members voted in favour.

questions.prompt: Which sentence expresses strong emphasis through litotes?
questions.explanation: *By no means trivial* = significant, stated with controlled understatement.
options: The difference is by no means trivial.
The difference is quite trivial indeed.

questions.prompt: Replace *very* with a precise collocation: *The committee was very worried about the delay.* (deep)
questions.explanation: *Deeply concerned/worried* is a natural, more formal collocation.
accepted: The committee was deeply concerned about the delay.
The committee was deeply worried about the delay.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Anticipatory it and there: extraposition and existential sentences: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: ___ essential that all participants sign the consent form.
questions.explanation: Anticipatory *it* for a that-clause subject.

questions.prompt: ___ several reasons why the project failed.
questions.explanation: Existential *there*; plural noun → *were*.

questions.prompt: Correct the sentence: *I find difficult to work in open-plan offices.*
questions.explanation: Object *it* after *find*.
accepted: I find it difficult to work in open-plan offices.

questions.prompt: Rewrite starting with *It*: *To ignore these warnings would be a mistake.*
questions.explanation: Extraposition of a to-infinitive subject.
accepted: It would be a mistake to ignore these warnings.

questions.prompt: Rewrite starting with *The bridge*: *It is thought that the bridge was built in the 12th century.*
questions.explanation: Personal passive + perfect passive infinitive for an earlier event.
accepted: The bridge is thought to have been built in the 12th century.

questions.prompt: There ___ (seem) to be a problem with your registration.
questions.explanation: *There seems to be* + singular noun.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the most cautious?
questions.explanation: *Would appear* and *may* combine two hedges.
options: It would appear that there may be grounds for concern.
It is clear that there are grounds for concern.
There is no doubt that there are grounds for concern.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is an *it*-cleft, not extraposition?
questions.explanation: Remove *It was ... that* and a full sentence remains: *The timing caused the problem.*
options: It was the timing that caused the problem.
It was obvious that the timing was wrong.
It is unclear whether the timing matters.
It surprised everyone that the timing changed.

questions.prompt: There ___ little doubt that the measures had some effect. (be, past)
questions.explanation: *There was little doubt that ...*: compact, confident claim.

questions.prompt: Rewrite with *There*: *Gold is said to be buried under the old mill.*
questions.explanation: Existential *there* + passive reporting verb + *to be*.
accepted: There is said to be gold buried under the old mill.

questions.prompt: Choose the most natural academic sentence.
questions.explanation: *It is worth noting that* is a standard academic frame.
options: It is worth noting that the data come from a single region.
That the data come from a single region is worth noting it.
There is worth noting that the data come from a single region.
Is worth to note that the data come from a single region.

questions.prompt: Move the heavy clause to the end: *A report that the company was in financial difficulty appeared in the press.*
questions.explanation: Extraposition from a noun phrase improves end-weight.
accepted: A report appeared in the press that the company was in financial difficulty.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Articles, countability, quantifiers and complex noun phrases: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: ___ is the most popular sport in Brazil.
questions.explanation: General reference to a sport → no article.

questions.prompt: I read ___ interesting article yesterday. ___ article was about sleep.
questions.explanation: First mention *an*, second mention *the*.

questions.prompt: Which part is incorrect? *The teacher gave us some useful advices before the exam.*
questions.explanation: *advice* is uncountable: *some useful advice*.

questions.prompt: There were ___ people at the concert, so it felt rather empty.
questions.explanation: *few* = not many (negative meaning); *people* is countable.

questions.prompt: My grandmother has been in ___ for a week. (as a patient) (write the article or – for none)
questions.explanation: Institution used for its purpose → no article (*in hospital*, BrE).

questions.prompt: Which is correct?
questions.explanation: Plural country names and rivers take *the*; lakes usually do not.
options: the Netherlands, the Danube, Lake Baikal
the Netherlands, Danube, the Lake Baikal

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: *evidence* is uncountable; *a body of evidence* is a natural academic phrase.
options: There is a growing body of evidence that diet affects mood.
There are a growing number of evidences that diet affects mood.
There is a growing number of evidence that diet affects mood.
There are many evidences that diet affects mood.

questions.prompt: Complete with 4–5 words. ‘House prices rose sharply, which surprised analysts.’ → ‘___ surprised analysts.’
questions.explanation: Nominalisation turns a clause into a noun phrase.
accepted: The sharp rise in house prices

questions.prompt: The flight was delayed for two hours. → It was a ___ delay.
questions.explanation: Compound adjective with a number: singular noun, hyphenated.

questions.prompt: ___ cheetah is the fastest land animal.
questions.explanation: Generic *the* + singular noun for a whole species (formal, encyclopaedic).

questions.prompt: ‘A significant ___ of research has examined the long-term effects of remote learning.’
questions.explanation: Uncountable *research* takes *a body of / an amount of*, not *a number of*.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Cohesion and reference: this, such, the former, summary nouns and given-new order: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: We compared trains and buses. ___ were faster but more expensive.
questions.explanation: *The former* = the first of two (trains).

questions.prompt: Inflation fell to 2% in March. ___ was welcomed by investors.
questions.explanation: Demonstrative + summary noun.

questions.prompt: ___ measures are rarely popular, but they can be effective. (one word)
questions.explanation: *Such* + plural noun.

questions.prompt: Correct the sentence: *There are four candidates, and the latter has the most experience.*
questions.explanation: *The latter* is used for the second of two only.
accepted: There are four candidates, and the last has the most experience.
There are four candidates, and the last one has the most experience.

questions.prompt: Which summary noun signals that the writer doubts the idea?
questions.explanation: *Claim* presents the idea as contestable.
options: This claim is not supported by the data.
This finding is supported by the data.
This result is supported by the data.
This fact is supported by the data.

questions.prompt: Rewrite using *respectively*: *The first group scored 61% and the second group scored 74%.*
questions.explanation: *Respectively* pairs two lists in order.
accepted: The first and second groups scored 61% and 74%, respectively.
The first and second groups scored 61% and 74% respectively.

questions.prompt: Many people plan to retire early, but few actually do ___.
questions.explanation: *Do so* replaces the verb phrase *retire early*.

questions.prompt: Which order follows the given-new principle best?
questions.explanation: The second sentence starts with given information (*this decision*) and ends with the new point.
options: The council approved the plan. This decision surprised residents.
The council approved the plan. Residents were surprised by the council approving the plan decision.
Residents surprised this decision of the council approving the plan.
The plan was approved. The surprise of residents was this decision.

questions.prompt: Which summary noun best encapsulates *Wealthier countries recycle more but also produce more waste*?
questions.explanation: *Paradox* captures the apparent contradiction.

questions.prompt: Choose the clearest academic continuation: *Participants who slept less made more errors. ___*
questions.explanation: A summary noun makes reference unambiguous.
options: This pattern held across all age groups.
This thing held across all of them.

questions.prompt: Correct the sentence: *Such a measures have been tried before.*
questions.explanation: *Such a* + singular; *such* + plural.
accepted: Such measures have been tried before.

questions.prompt: Make the reference clear with a summary noun: *Prices rose while demand fell. This worried the board.*
questions.explanation: A summary noun specifies what *this* refers to.
accepted: Prices rose while demand fell. This combination worried the board.
Prices rose while demand fell. This combination of trends worried the board.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Comparison, degree and modification: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: The train is ___ faster than the bus; it takes half the time.
questions.explanation: *much/far* modify comparatives; *very* does not.

questions.prompt: This is the ___ (bad) film I've ever seen.
questions.explanation: Irregular superlative.

questions.prompt: Which part is incorrect? *My new flat is more bigger than my old one and closer to work.*
questions.explanation: Double comparative → *bigger*.

questions.prompt: Complete with 3 words. ‘The more you read, the better your vocabulary becomes.’ → ‘___ read, the better your vocabulary becomes.’ (keep the same structure)
questions.explanation: *the + comparative, the + comparative*.

questions.prompt: Complete with 4 words. ‘Petrol costs double what it cost in 2015.’ → ‘Petrol costs ___ it did in 2015.’
questions.explanation: *twice as much as* for multiples.

questions.prompt: Tokyo is ___ the largest city in the world by population.
questions.explanation: *by far* modifies superlatives.

questions.prompt: The new policy was ___ as effective as the government claimed. (big difference)
questions.explanation: *nowhere near as … as* = much less … than.

questions.prompt: ‘Salaries in the region are now on a ___ with those in the capital.’
questions.explanation: *on a par with* = at the same level as.

questions.prompt: Choose the best sentence for describing a chart.
questions.explanation: Precise adverbs (*slightly, sharply*) and *whereas* for contrast.
options: Sales rose slightly in March, whereas profits fell sharply.
Sales rose a bit in March, but profits went really down.
Sales very rose in March, while profits fell very.
Sales rose slightly in March, whereas profits fell sharp.

questions.prompt: Please contact us if you require ___ information.
questions.explanation: *further* = additional; *farther* is only for distance.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Conditionals, wishes and the unreal past: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: If you ___ water to 100°C, it boils.
questions.explanation: General truth → zero conditional (present + present).

questions.prompt: If we ___ (leave) ten minutes earlier, we would have caught the train.
questions.explanation: Unreal past → past perfect in the if-clause.

questions.prompt: If I had studied medicine, I ___ a doctor now.
questions.explanation: Past condition, present result → mixed conditional.

questions.prompt: You can borrow my car ___ you fill it up afterwards.
questions.explanation: *as long as* = only if (a condition).

questions.prompt: Take some cash ___ the card machine isn't working.
questions.explanation: A precaution, not a condition → *in case*.

questions.prompt: I wish I ___ (not / say) that to her yesterday.
questions.explanation: Past regret → wish + past perfect.

questions.prompt: It's high time the government ___ (do) something about housing.
questions.explanation: *It's (high) time* + past simple for something that should already happen.

questions.prompt: Which part is incorrect? *Unless you don't book now, there won't be any seats left.*
questions.explanation: *Unless* already means *if not*: *Unless you book now…*

questions.prompt: Complete with 3 words (formal inversion). ‘If I had known about the strike, I would have driven.’ → ‘___ about the strike, I would have driven.’
questions.explanation: Inverted third conditional: *Had* + subject + past participle.

questions.prompt: Complete with 4 words. ‘Your support was the only reason we succeeded.’ → ‘___ your support, we would not have succeeded.’
questions.explanation: *If it hadn't been for / But for* + noun = without.
accepted: If it had not been for

questions.prompt: I'd rather you ___ my phone without asking.
questions.explanation: *would rather* + another subject + past simple.

questions.prompt: ‘___ any further information be required, please do not hesitate to contact us.’
questions.explanation: Inverted first conditional in formal letters: *Should* + subject + infinitive.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Dependent prepositions after verbs, adjectives and nouns: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: The price ___ the size of the room.
questions.explanation: *depend on* is fixed.

questions.prompt: She apologised ___ being late.
questions.explanation: *apologise (to sb) for sth*

questions.prompt: He's very good ___ explaining complicated ideas.
questions.explanation: *good at* + noun / -ing

questions.prompt: Correct the mistake: "We discussed about the new timetable."
questions.explanation: *discuss* has no preposition.

questions.prompt: There has been a sharp increase ___ the number of cyclists.
questions.explanation: *an increase in* + the thing that rises

questions.prompt: Most members agreed ___ the proposal to extend opening hours.
questions.explanation: *agree to* a proposal or plan; *agree with* a person or opinion.

questions.prompt: Correct the mistake: "Social media has a big impact to teenagers."
questions.explanation: *impact on*
accepted: Social media has a big impact on teenagers.

questions.prompt: I'm thinking ___ (apply) for a master's degree.
questions.explanation: Preposition + -ing.

questions.prompt: Many health problems result ___ poor diet.
questions.explanation: *result from* = be caused by; *result in* = cause.

questions.prompt: Make more formal: "These are the conditions they work under."
questions.explanation: Formal style: preposition + *which*.
accepted: These are the conditions under which they work.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Ellipsis and substitution: leaving words out and replacing them: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: "Do you think it'll snow?" "I don't think ___."
questions.explanation: After *think*, *so* replaces the whole clause (*it'll snow*).

questions.prompt: "Will the shop be open?" "I'm afraid ___."
questions.explanation: Negative with *be afraid*: *I'm afraid not.*

questions.prompt: Correct the mistake: "Is it going to be expensive?" "I don't hope so."
questions.explanation: *Hope* is not used with *don't … so*; say *I hope not*.

questions.prompt: These glasses are too small. Have you got any bigger ___?
questions.explanation: *ones* replaces a plural countable noun (*glasses*).

questions.prompt: I lost my phone yesterday but luckily I found ___ in my coat.
questions.explanation: *it* refers to the same phone; *one* would mean a different phone.

questions.prompt: I didn't want to sign the contract, but in the end I had ___.
questions.explanation: Keep *to* when the verb after it is left out.

questions.prompt: Rewrite more formally: "If you want to complain, you can complain online." (use DO SO)
questions.explanation: *Do so* replaces the repeated verb phrase in formal English.
accepted: If you want to complain, you can do so online.
If you wish to complain, you can do so online.

questions.prompt: "Have you ever been to Peru?" "Yes, I ___."
questions.explanation: Keep the first auxiliary from the question: *have*.

questions.prompt: Correct the mistake: "He's left the company." "Yes, I know so."
questions.explanation: *Know* doesn't take *so*.

questions.prompt: Some cities invested heavily in cycling infrastructure; ___ did not, and saw little change.
questions.explanation: *others* = other cities; the verb phrase is substituted by *did not*.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Future forms, probability and time clauses: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: Look out! That glass ___ fall off the table.
questions.explanation: Present evidence for a prediction → *be going to*.

questions.prompt: I can't come on Friday. I ___ my grandparents; we booked the tickets weeks ago.
questions.explanation: Fixed personal arrangement → present continuous.

questions.prompt: I'll text you as soon as the results ___ (come) out.
questions.explanation: Time clause about the future → present simple.

questions.prompt: By the time you read this letter, I ___ (leave) the country.
questions.explanation: Completed before a future point → future perfect.

questions.prompt: Don't phone at eight. We ___ dinner then.
questions.explanation: In progress at a future moment → future continuous.

questions.prompt: Which part is incorrect? *Once the contract will be signed, we will start the project.*
questions.explanation: Time clause → *Once the contract is signed / has been signed*.

questions.prompt: Which sentence expresses the LOWEST probability?
questions.explanation: *I doubt whether* = unlikely; *bound to* = almost certain.
options: I doubt whether prices will fall this year.
Prices are likely to fall this year.
Prices are bound to fall this year.

questions.prompt: Complete with 3 words. ‘The minister will visit the region next week (official plan).’ → ‘The minister ___ the region next week.’
questions.explanation: *be to* + infinitive for formal, official arrangements.

questions.prompt: The meeting ___ start at ten, but the chairman's flight has been delayed.
questions.explanation: Future in the past for a scheduled event that may not happen → *was due to*.

questions.prompt: Complete in an academic style: ‘Global demand for lithium ___ (expect) to triple by 2030.’
questions.explanation: Impersonal passive for forecasts: *is expected to*.

questions.prompt: ‘The company is on the ___ of collapse; analysts give it weeks.’
questions.explanation: *on the verge / brink / point of* + noun or -ing = about to happen.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: The future in the past: was going to, was to, was about to, would: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: Nobody imagined that the small start-up ___ a global company.
questions.explanation: Prediction from a past viewpoint → *would*.

questions.prompt: I ___ you, but my battery died.
questions.explanation: Unfulfilled intention → *was going to*.

questions.prompt: We were ___ point of giving up when the results finally came in. (two words)
questions.explanation: *Be on the point of* + -ing = about to.

questions.prompt: Rewrite to show the event did not happen, using *was to have*: *The prime minister was going to open the new hospital, but she was ill.*
questions.explanation: *Was to have* + past participle = planned but not realised.
accepted: The prime minister was to have opened the new hospital, but she was ill.

questions.prompt: Correct the sentence: *I was sure that the results will be positive.*
questions.explanation: Past viewpoint: *will* → *would*.
accepted: I was sure that the results would be positive.

questions.prompt: In which sentence is *would* a past habit, not the future in the past?
questions.explanation: Repeated past behaviour.
options: Every evening she would walk along the river.
She knew the walk would take an hour.
He promised he would walk her home.
They hoped the weather would be fine for the walk.

questions.prompt: We ___ (about) to start the experiment when the power went off.
questions.explanation: *Were about to* + *when* for interrupted imminent action.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is typical of historical narrative?
questions.explanation: *Was to* = destiny seen from the past.
options: The treaty was to shape European politics for decades.
The treaty is going to shape European politics for decades.
The treaty would shaped European politics for decades.
The treaty was shaping European politics for decades tomorrow.

questions.prompt: Rewrite with inversion beginning *Little*: *They didn't realise that the project would take a decade.*
questions.explanation: Negative adverbial *little* + inversion.
accepted: Little did they realise that the project would take a decade.

questions.prompt: By the end of the year, she hoped, she ___ (finish) her thesis.
questions.explanation: Future perfect in the past.

questions.prompt: Choose the best continuation: *The decision seemed minor at the time, but it ___*
questions.explanation: Foreshadowing with *would*.

questions.prompt: Report the promise: *"I'll send the documents tomorrow," he said.*
questions.explanation: *Will → would*; *tomorrow → the next/following day*.
accepted: He said he would send the documents the next day.
He said that he would send the documents the next day.
He said he would send the documents the following day.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Habits: used to, would, be used to and will: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: When I was a teenager, I ___ a motorbike.
questions.explanation: *have* (= own) is a state, so *would* is not possible.

questions.prompt: I've lived in Manchester for years, so I ___ the rain.
questions.explanation: Familiarity → *be used to* + noun.

questions.prompt: It took me ages to get used to ___ (drive) on the left.
questions.explanation: *get used to* + -ing.

questions.prompt: Which part is incorrect? *Did you used to walk to school when you were little?*
questions.explanation: In questions: *Did you use to…?*

questions.prompt: Every evening my grandfather ___ the newspaper aloud to us.
questions.explanation: Repeated past action in a nostalgic narrative → *would*.

questions.prompt: I ___ to Prague four times as a student.
questions.explanation: A specific number of times → past simple, not a habit form.

questions.prompt: Complete with 3–4 words. ‘Working at night still feels strange to me.’ → ‘I'm ___ at night yet.’
questions.explanation: Not yet familiar → *not used to* + -ing.

questions.prompt: ‘You ___ leaving your wet towels on the floor!’ (irritated)
questions.explanation: *always* + present continuous expresses irritation at a repeated habit.

questions.prompt: ‘She failed again? Well, she ___ refuse to take advice.’ (typical, annoying behaviour)
questions.explanation: Stressed *will/would* for characteristic, often irritating behaviour.

questions.prompt: Rewrite more formally: ‘In the past, families used to eat together.’ → ‘Families ___ ate together.’
questions.explanation: Formal writing prefers adverbs such as *traditionally* or *formerly*.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Indirect questions and question tags: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: Could you tell me where ___?
questions.explanation: Indirect questions use statement word order.

questions.prompt: Make polite: "What time does the meeting start?" (Do you know…)
questions.explanation: Remove *does* and use statement order: *the meeting starts*.
accepted: Do you know what time the meeting starts?

questions.prompt: She doesn't eat meat, ___ she?
questions.explanation: Negative statement → positive tag with the same auxiliary.

questions.prompt: I'm on the list, ___?
questions.explanation: The standard tag for *I am* is *aren't I?*

questions.prompt: Let's take a taxi, ___ we?
questions.explanation: Tag after *Let's* is *shall we?*

questions.prompt: Correct the mistake: "I wonder what does this word mean."
questions.explanation: No *does*; statement order *this word means*.
accepted: I wonder what this word means.

questions.prompt: Nobody saw the accident, ___?
questions.explanation: *Nobody* makes the sentence negative, so the tag is positive; we use *they*.

questions.prompt: Write a formal request: "When will the results be available?" (I'd be grateful if you could let me know…)
questions.explanation: Statement order: *the results will be available*.
accepted: I'd be grateful if you could let me know when the results will be available.

questions.prompt: There was a long debate about ___ to raise the speed limit.
questions.explanation: Use *whether* after a preposition and before a *to*-infinitive.

questions.prompt: (Seeing someone with a guitar) "So you play in a band, ___?" — showing interest, not a real question.
questions.explanation: A same-polarity tag (*play… do you?*) expresses interest or surprise.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Emphasis: cleft sentences, inversion, fronting and auxiliary do: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: ___ I need is a long holiday.
questions.explanation: What-cleft: *What I need is…*

questions.prompt: It ___ my sister who told me the news, not my mother.
questions.explanation: It-cleft: *It was* + focus + *who*.

questions.prompt: “You didn't lock the door!” “I ___ lock it! I remember doing it.”
questions.explanation: Emphatic *did* contradicts.

questions.prompt: Rarely ___ such a talented young pianist.
questions.explanation: Negative adverbial first → auxiliary + subject.

questions.prompt: Complete with 3–4 words. ‘She won the race and she also broke the record.’ → ‘Not only ___ the race, but she also broke the record.’
questions.explanation: *Not only* + inversion with *did*.

questions.prompt: Which part is incorrect? *Only when the results were published the scientists realised their error.*
questions.explanation: Invert the main clause: *did the scientists realise*.

questions.prompt: Complete with 4 words. ‘You must not open this door in any situation.’ → ‘Under no ___ open this door.’
questions.explanation: *Under no circumstances* + inversion.

questions.prompt: Complete with 4 words. ‘We only realised how serious it was at midnight.’ → ‘It ___ midnight that we realised how serious it was.’
questions.explanation: *It was not until…that* emphasises the time.

questions.prompt: ___, I can't agree with the decision.
questions.explanation: Concessive fronting: *Much as* + clause = although I respect her a lot.
options: However much I am respecting her

questions.prompt: ‘So ___ the demand that tickets sold out in minutes.’
questions.explanation: *So* + adjective + inversion (*was the demand*) for emphasis.

questions.prompt: Write the missing word for an academic sentence: ‘It is ___ assumption that this study sets out to challenge.’
questions.explanation: It-cleft focusing on a specific idea already introduced.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Linking ideas: contrast, concession, cause and result: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: ___ the heavy traffic, we arrived on time.
questions.explanation: *Despite* + noun phrase.

questions.prompt: ___ he had trained for months, he didn't finish the marathon.
questions.explanation: Conjunction + clause for concession.

questions.prompt: Which part is incorrect? *In spite of it was raining, the festival went ahead as planned.*
questions.explanation: *In spite of* + noun/-ing: *In spite of the rain / In spite of it raining*.
options: In spite of it was raining

questions.prompt: The flight was delayed ___ a technical problem.
questions.explanation: *because of* + noun.

questions.prompt: My brother loves crowds, ___ I prefer quiet places.
questions.explanation: *whereas* contrasts two facts in one sentence.

questions.prompt: “Was the lecture boring?” “No. ___, it was the best I've attended.”
questions.explanation: *On the contrary* rejects the previous idea.

questions.prompt: Complete with 3–4 words. ‘Because the evidence was weak, the case was dropped.’ → ‘The case was dropped ___ the weak evidence.’
questions.explanation: Preposition + noun phrase for cause.

questions.prompt: Join with *Despite the fact*: ‘Prices rose. Demand increased.’ → ‘___ that prices rose, demand increased.’
questions.explanation: *Despite the fact that* + clause.

questions.prompt: Complete with 3 words. ‘Although it may be difficult, we must act now.’ → ‘Difficult ___ be, we must act now.’
questions.explanation: Fronted concession: adjective + *though/as* + subject + verb.

questions.prompt: Which linker is most appropriate in a formal report? ‘Costs rose sharply. ___, the project was suspended.’
questions.explanation: Formal result adverb.

questions.prompt: ‘The plan has some merit. Be that as it ___, it is far too expensive.’
questions.explanation: *Be that as it may* = even so (formal concession).

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Modals: obligation, deduction and stance: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: In many countries you ___ carry an ID card; it's the law.
questions.explanation: An external rule → *have to*.

questions.prompt: You ___ bring food; lunch is included.
questions.explanation: No obligation, not prohibition.

questions.prompt: The lights are off. They ___ (be) out.
questions.explanation: Logical certainty in the present → *must be*.

questions.prompt: She ___ (see) the email; she replied within minutes. (certain)
questions.explanation: Certainty about the past → *must have* + V3.

questions.prompt: He ___ written this report: it's full of errors, and he's very careful.
questions.explanation: Sure something is NOT true in the past → *can't have*.

questions.prompt: We bought a new heater, but we ___. The weather turned warm the next day.
questions.explanation: We did it, but it was unnecessary → *needn't have (bought)*.

questions.prompt: Which part is incorrect? *Despite the storm, we could reach the summit before dark.*
questions.explanation: Specific achievement in the past → *managed to reach / were able to reach*.

questions.prompt: Complete with 3 words. ‘It is very probable that the trial will be postponed.’ → ‘In ___, the trial will be postponed.’
questions.explanation: *In all likelihood/probability* = very probably.

questions.prompt: It is essential that every applicant ___ two references.
questions.explanation: Formal subjunctive after *essential/imperative/vital that*: base form.

questions.prompt: Hedge this claim for an essay: ‘These results ___ suggest that diet affects mood.’ (tentative)
questions.explanation: Hedging with a weak modal or *would seem to* makes academic claims appropriately cautious.

questions.prompt: ‘You ___ have told me you were vegetarian! I'd have cooked something else.’
questions.explanation: *could have* + V3 as a reproach: it was possible, but you didn't.

questions.prompt: ‘Whether the reforms will work ___ to be seen.’
questions.explanation: *It remains to be seen whether…* = it is not yet known.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Multi-word verbs: phrasal and prepositional verbs, word order and register: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: The meeting was cancelled. They called ___.
questions.explanation: Pronoun object between verb and adverb particle.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: *Look at* is prepositional: the object follows the preposition.

questions.prompt: Correct the sentence: *I'm looking forward to see the results.*
questions.explanation: *To* is a preposition: use the -ing form.
accepted: I'm looking forward to seeing the results.
I am looking forward to seeing the results.

questions.prompt: Unemployment has fallen, but the government's critics point ___ that wages are still low.
questions.explanation: *Point out* = draw attention to.

questions.prompt: The strike was a serious ___ for the negotiations.
questions.explanation: Noun from *set back*.

questions.prompt: Rewrite in the passive: *The committee turned down the proposal.*
questions.explanation: Passive of a separable phrasal verb keeps the particle after the participle.
accepted: The proposal was turned down by the committee.

questions.prompt: Which version suits an academic report?
questions.explanation: *Carry out* is an established academic phrasal verb.
options: The study was carried out over two years.
The study was done over two years, more or less.
The study got done over two years.
The study was sorted out over two years.

questions.prompt: These findings are ___ out by later research. (= confirmed)
questions.explanation: *Bear out* = confirm; passive *be borne out*.

questions.prompt: "Women make up 60% of the workforce." What does *make up* mean here?
questions.explanation: *Make up* = form or constitute a proportion.

questions.prompt: Several factors may have contributed, but we can ___ out human error, as the system was fully automated.
questions.explanation: *Rule out* = exclude as a possibility.

questions.prompt: Choose the best replacement for the informal phrase in an essay: *Governments should **get rid of** these subsidies.*
questions.explanation: *Abolish* is the formal equivalent for laws and subsidies.

questions.prompt: Replace the verb with a phrasal verb using *stem*: *The problem originates from poor communication.*
questions.explanation: *Stem from* = originate in; academic.
accepted: The problem stems from poor communication.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Narrative tenses and the past perfect: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: By the time the ambulance arrived, the man ___.
questions.explanation: *By the time* + past → the earlier event takes the past perfect.

questions.prompt: I ___ (walk) home when it started to pour with rain.
questions.explanation: An action in progress interrupted by another → past continuous.

questions.prompt: She looked exhausted because she ___ (work) all night.
questions.explanation: Cause of a visible past result, with duration → past perfect continuous.

questions.prompt: When we got to the cinema, the film ___, so we missed the beginning.
questions.explanation: The film started before we arrived → past perfect.

questions.prompt: Which part is incorrect? *After the guests had left, we had cleaned the whole flat.*
questions.explanation: Only the earlier event needs the past perfect: *we cleaned*.

questions.prompt: I ___ call you last night, but my phone died.
questions.explanation: A plan that did not happen → *was going to*.

questions.prompt: Complete with 4 words. ‘As soon as we sat down, the alarm went off.’ → ‘No sooner ___ than the alarm went off.’
questions.explanation: *No sooner* at the start triggers inversion with the past perfect.

questions.prompt: Choose the best sentence for a history essay.
questions.explanation: *By* + past time → past perfect for completion before that point.
options: By the end of the decade, the industry had collapsed.
By the end of the decade, the industry collapses.
By the end of the decade, the industry has collapsed.
By the end of the decade, the industry was collapsing already.

questions.prompt: Rewrite with a perfect infinitive: ‘People say that he left the country.’ → ‘He is said ___ the country.’
questions.explanation: A past event after a present reporting verb → *to have* + past participle.

questions.prompt: ‘Hardly ___ the door when the phone rang.’ (I / close)
questions.explanation: *Hardly … when* takes inversion and the past perfect.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Negation, scope and focusing adverbs: not, no, hardly, only, even: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: Which sentence means that some students failed?
questions.explanation: *Not all* = partial negation.

questions.prompt: Choose the most natural sentence.
questions.explanation: Negative transfer with *think*.
options: I don't think the deadline is realistic.
I think the deadline isn't realistic.
I think not the deadline is realistic.
I don't think the deadline isn't realistic.

questions.prompt: She rarely makes mistakes, ___ she? (auxiliary)
questions.explanation: After *rarely* the tag is positive.

questions.prompt: Correct the sentence: *I didn't enjoy the film too.*
questions.explanation: Negative addition uses *either*.
accepted: I didn't enjoy the film either.

questions.prompt: "There is ___ time left, so we must hurry."
questions.explanation: *Little* (uncountable, negative meaning: not enough).

questions.prompt: Make the scope clear: *We only interviewed managers.* (so that *only* applies to *managers*)
questions.explanation: Place *only* directly before the focused element.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is a cautious way of saying *quite common*?
questions.explanation: Litotes: negating a negative adjective.
options: The problem is not at all common.

questions.prompt: Rewrite with inversion: *The minister did not apologise at any point.* Begin: *At no point ...*
questions.explanation: Negative adverbial + auxiliary inversion.
accepted: At no point did the minister apologise.

questions.prompt: "This does not necessarily mean that the policy failed." What is being denied?
questions.explanation: *Not necessarily* denies necessity, not the possibility.
options: That the conclusion "the policy failed" must follow.
That there is any meaning at all.

questions.prompt: Only after the third trial ___ the researchers notice the pattern. (auxiliary)
questions.explanation: Fronted *only* + time expression triggers inversion.

questions.prompt: Which phrase presents 12% as disappointingly small?
questions.explanation: *Just* minimises; the others emphasise size.
options: The scheme reached just 12% of households.
The scheme reached as many as 12% of households.
The scheme reached a full 12% of households.
The scheme reached no fewer than 12% of households.

questions.prompt: Correct the double negative: *Nobody didn't say nothing about it.*
questions.explanation: Standard English allows one negative per clause.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Noun clauses: that-clauses, wh-clauses and whether: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: I'd like to know ___.
questions.explanation: Statement order inside a wh-clause.
options: what time does the meeting start
what time the meeting does start

questions.prompt: We haven't decided ___ to accept the offer.
questions.explanation: Before a to-infinitive only *whether* is possible.

questions.prompt: She was upset by ___ that nobody had thanked her. (two words)
questions.explanation: After a preposition, use *the fact that*.

questions.prompt: Correct the sentence: *Can you tell me where is the library?*
questions.explanation: Indirect wh-clause → statement order.
accepted: Can you tell me where the library is?

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct and natural?
questions.explanation: Complement position after *is*: *whether* is preferred in writing.
options: What matters most is whether the system is fair.
What matters most is if the system is fair.
That matters most is whether the system is fair.
What matters most whether the system is fair.

questions.prompt: Rewrite with *It*: *That the treatment was effective is evident from the data.*
questions.explanation: Long subject that-clauses are usually extraposed.
accepted: It is evident from the data that the treatment was effective.

questions.prompt: In which sentence is *that* a relative pronoun (replaceable by *which*)?
questions.explanation: In the first sentence *that* is the object of *proposed*. In the others, the clause gives the content of the noun (appositive).
options: The theory that he proposed was later disproved.
The theory that the universe is expanding is widely accepted.
The belief that hard work always pays off is naive.
The claim that prices will fall is unconvincing.

questions.prompt: ___ some students thrive under pressure while others struggle is still poorly understood. (one word)
questions.explanation: A wh-clause as subject.

questions.prompt: Rewrite as a pseudo-cleft beginning *What*: *The evidence suggests that the effect fades over time.*
questions.explanation: *What* + clause + *is* + that-clause.
accepted: What the evidence suggests is that the effect fades over time.

questions.prompt: Choose the most concise formal version.
questions.explanation: Prefer *although* over a wordy *the fact that* construction.
options: Although the sample was small, the findings are robust.
Due to the fact that the sample was small, the findings are robust.
In spite of the fact of the sample being small, the findings are robust.
Despite of the fact that the sample was small, the findings are robust.

questions.prompt: Correct the sentence: *The question if the results can be generalised remains open.*
questions.explanation: After a noun, use *(of) whether*.
accepted: The question of whether the results can be generalised remains open.
The question whether the results can be generalised remains open.

questions.prompt: Much depends ___ whether the reforms are implemented consistently.
questions.explanation: *Depend on* + whether-clause.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Participle clauses and reduced relative clauses: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: ___ the instructions, I couldn't assemble the desk.
questions.explanation: Negative perfect participle for an earlier action that explains the result.

questions.prompt: The students ___ the exam early were allowed to leave.
questions.explanation: Active meaning → present participle (= who finished).

questions.prompt: Most of the goods ___ (produce) in the factory are exported.
questions.explanation: Passive meaning → past participle (= which are produced).

questions.prompt: She was the first woman ___ the prize.
questions.explanation: After *the first/last/only* → to-infinitive.

questions.prompt: Which part is incorrect? *Turning the corner, the museum came into view and we stopped.*
questions.explanation: Dangling participle: the museum didn't turn the corner. *Turning the corner, we saw the museum.*
options: Turning the corner, the museum came into view

questions.prompt: Complete with 3 words. ‘Because he had been warned about the traffic, he left early.’ → ‘___ about the traffic, he left early.’
questions.explanation: Passive perfect participle for an earlier action done to the subject.

questions.prompt: ___ correctly, this medicine has very few side effects.
questions.explanation: Condition with passive meaning (= if it is taken).

questions.prompt: Rewrite with *with*: ‘Because unemployment is rising, the government is under pressure.’ → ‘___ rising, the government is under pressure.’
questions.explanation: *With* + noun + participle gives background or reason.

questions.prompt: Academic style: ‘___ (draw) on interviews with 50 nurses, the study explores burnout.’
questions.explanation: Active participle clause at the start of an academic sentence.

questions.prompt: ‘Weather ___, the ceremony will take place outdoors.’
questions.explanation: Absolute participle clause: *weather permitting* = if the weather allows.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: The passive, impersonal passives and the causative: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: The new hospital ___ next year.
questions.explanation: Future passive: *will be* + past participle.

questions.prompt: Our flat ___ (redecorate) at the moment, so we're staying with friends.
questions.explanation: Present continuous passive: *is being* + V3.

questions.prompt: Which part is incorrect? *The accident was happened at around midnight on the ring road.*
questions.explanation: *happen* is intransitive and has no passive: *The accident happened…*

questions.prompt: Complete with 3 words. ‘People believe that the ship sank in a storm.’ → ‘The ship is ___ in a storm.’
questions.explanation: Subject + passive reporting verb + perfect infinitive for a past event.

questions.prompt: Complete with 3–4 words. ‘Reports say the president is considering a new cabinet.’ → ‘The president is ___ a new cabinet.’
questions.explanation: Ongoing action → *to be* + -ing.

questions.prompt: I didn't fix the roof myself. I ___.
questions.explanation: Causative: *have* + object + past participle.

questions.prompt: Most people hate ___ (keep) waiting.
questions.explanation: After *hate* → -ing; passive -ing = *being* + V3.

questions.prompt: The documents need ___ before the deadline.
questions.explanation: Passive infinitive after *need* (or *need signing* in BrE).

questions.prompt: ‘My uncle ___ his wallet stolen while he was on holiday.’ (unpleasant experience)
questions.explanation: *have/get something done* can describe something bad that happened to you.

questions.prompt: Make this sentence impersonal for an essay: ‘Many experts argue that tourism harms local culture.’ → ‘It ___ that tourism harms local culture.’
questions.explanation: Impersonal passive with *It* distances the writer from the claim.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is most appropriate in a methods section?
questions.explanation: Formal passive without the agent focuses on the procedure; *got* is too informal.
options: Participants were randomly assigned to two groups.
We randomly put people into two groups.
People got randomly assigned to two groups.
Two groups were randomly assigned participants by us.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Present perfect and aspect: simple, continuous and perfect forms: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: I ___ to Japan three times, but never in winter.
questions.explanation: Experience in an unfinished period (my life) → present perfect *have been*. *Have gone* would mean I am still there.

questions.prompt: I ___ (live) in Kazan since I was a child.
questions.explanation: *since* + point in time and the situation continues → present perfect (simple or continuous).

questions.prompt: Your hands are covered in paint! What ___?
questions.explanation: The paint is visible evidence of a recent activity → present perfect continuous.

questions.prompt: Which part is incorrect? *When have you arrived in Vienna? I didn't see you at the meeting.*
questions.explanation: *When* asks about a finished time → *When did you arrive?*

questions.prompt: She's a fast writer: she ___ (write) four chapters this month.
questions.explanation: A completed number → present perfect simple, not continuous.

questions.prompt: Complete with 3–4 words so the meaning stays the same. ‘I started working here three years ago.’ → ‘I ___ for three years.’
questions.explanation: *started … ago* → present perfect with *for* + period.

questions.prompt: This is the first time I ___ a speech in English.
questions.explanation: *This is the first time…* is followed by the present perfect.

questions.prompt: Which sentence sounds most tentative and polite in an email to a professor?
questions.explanation: The past continuous *I was wondering* distances the request and softens it.
options: I was wondering whether you might have time to read my draft.
I wonder whether you have time to read my draft.
I wondered whether you had time to read my draft.
Do you have time to read my draft?

questions.prompt: Choose the best opening for a literature review.
questions.explanation: Summarising research up to the present → present perfect.
options: A number of studies have investigated the effects of screen time on sleep.
A number of studies investigated the effects of screen time on sleep last year.
A number of studies are investigating the effects of screen time on sleep since 2010.
A number of studies investigate the effects of screen time on sleep until now.

questions.prompt: Rewrite using a perfect participle (begin with *Having*). ‘After she had checked the data, she submitted the paper.’ → ‘___ the data, she submitted the paper.’
questions.explanation: A perfect participle clause shows that one action was completed before the next.

questions.prompt: ‘I ___ to ring you for weeks, but something always gets in the way.’ (an intention not yet carried out)
questions.explanation: *mean* in the perfect continuous expresses a long-standing intention not yet fulfilled.

questions.prompt: Which part is incorrect? *Researchers have been knowing for decades that the drug has side effects.*
questions.explanation: *know* is a state verb → *have known*.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Perfect and passive infinitives and -ing forms: to have done, being done, having been done: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: Which sentence shows that the action happened before the time of believing?
questions.explanation: A perfect infinitive (*to have escaped*) places the escape before the present belief.
options: The thieves are believed to have escaped by boat.
The thieves are believed to escape by boat.
The thieves are believed escaping by boat.
The thieves are believed to be escaping by boat.

questions.prompt: I really dislike ___ (treat) like a child by my manager.
questions.explanation: Passive meaning after a verb that takes -ing: *being* + past participle.

questions.prompt: The palace is thought ___ (build) in the early 1600s.
questions.explanation: Present belief about a past event, and the palace was built by someone: perfect passive infinitive.

questions.prompt: Rewrite using the personal passive: *People say that the director is planning a sequel.*
questions.explanation: Ongoing action at the time of saying: continuous infinitive.
accepted: The director is said to be planning a sequel.

questions.prompt: Which sentence expresses regret about something that did NOT happen?
questions.explanation: *Would like* + perfect infinitive describes an unfulfilled past wish.
options: I would like to have met your parents.
I would like to meet your parents.
I like to have met your parents.
I would like meeting your parents.

questions.prompt: Correct the sentence: *Having been delayed for six hours, the passengers' patience ran out.*
questions.explanation: The perfect participle clause must share its subject with the main clause: the passengers were delayed, not their patience.
accepted: Having been delayed for six hours, the passengers ran out of patience.

questions.prompt: He strongly denied ___ (involve) in the scandal.
questions.explanation: Passive meaning after *deny*; the perfect form stresses that the involvement was earlier.

questions.prompt: Which version is most typical of a formal news report?
questions.explanation: Passive reporting + perfect passive infinitive is compact and impersonal.
options: Three people are reported to have been injured in the explosion.
They are saying three people got hurt in the explosion.
Three people, it is reported, they were injured in the explosion.
Three people are reported being injured in the explosion.

questions.prompt: Rewrite with a perfect participle clause: *She had studied the data carefully, and then she rejected the hypothesis.*
questions.explanation: *Having* + past participle shows the earlier, completed action; the subject is shared.
accepted: Having studied the data carefully, she rejected the hypothesis.

questions.prompt: What does the sentence imply? *The new terminal was to have opened in March.*
questions.explanation: *Was to have* + past participle describes a plan that was not fulfilled.
options: The terminal did not open in March as planned.
The terminal opened in March as planned.
Nobody knows when the terminal will open.
The terminal had already opened before March.

questions.prompt: The effect appears ___ (overestimate) in several earlier studies.
questions.explanation: Earlier time + passive meaning: perfect passive infinitive, used for cautious academic reporting.

questions.prompt: Choose the best completion for formal narrative: *Rejected by three publishers, the novel finally appeared in 1952, ___ by critics but largely ignored by readers.*
questions.explanation: An infinitive of outcome presents a later (often ironic) result: *to be praised*.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Prepositional phrases: fixed expressions beginning with a preposition: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: I'm afraid a pay rise is out of the ___ this year.
questions.explanation: *out of the question* = impossible.

questions.prompt: I didn't do it on ___ — it was an accident.
questions.explanation: *on purpose* = deliberately.

questions.prompt: We got to the station just in ___ to catch the last train.
questions.explanation: *in time (to do sth)* = early enough.

questions.prompt: Correct the mistake: "At the end, they agreed to sell the house."
questions.explanation: *In the end* = finally.
accepted: In the end, they agreed to sell the house.
In the end they agreed to sell the house.

questions.prompt: She spoke on ___ of all the volunteers.
questions.explanation: *on behalf of* = representing.

questions.prompt: "Was the film boring?" "On the ___, it was gripping from start to finish."
questions.explanation: *On the contrary* rejects the previous idea.

questions.prompt: Correct the mistake: "Who is in charge for the budget?"
questions.explanation: *in charge of*
accepted: Who is in charge of the budget?

questions.prompt: The application was refused on the ___ that it was incomplete.
questions.explanation: *on the grounds that* + clause.

questions.prompt: Economic growth often comes at the ___ of the environment.
questions.explanation: *at the expense of* = causing harm to.

questions.prompt: ___ these findings, the committee decided to postpone the decision.
questions.explanation: *In the light of* = considering.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Punctuation for clear academic writing: practice
instructions: Mixed practice from B2 to C2. Every explanation links back to the rule it practises.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
questions.explanation: Two complete sentences: use a semicolon or full stop, not a comma alone (comma splice).
options: The museum was closed; we visited the park instead.
The museum was closed, we visited the park instead.
The museum was closed we visited the park instead.
The museum, was closed; we visited the park instead.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct punctuation: ‘Sales increased in March ___ they fell again in April.’
questions.explanation: A comma + coordinating conjunction (*but*) can join two full clauses. *However* would need a semicolon before it.

questions.prompt: Prices rose sharply ___ demand remained stable.
questions.explanation: *However* joining two clauses: semicolon before, comma after.

questions.prompt: Which sentence needs NO comma?
questions.explanation: A defining relative clause identifies the noun, so it takes no commas.
options: Students who miss the deadline will lose marks.
Although it was late, the meeting continued.
The report, which was published in May, was widely read.

questions.prompt: Which use of the colon is correct?
questions.explanation: A colon must follow a complete clause and introduce an explanation, list or quotation.
options: The plan has one weakness: it is too expensive.
The reasons for the decision were: cost and time.
We need to buy: paper, pens and folders.
She said: that she would come later.

questions.prompt: Write the correct form: ‘The ___ (company) profits fell, but its employees kept their jobs.’
questions.explanation: Singular possession: *company's*.

questions.prompt: Write the correct form: ‘All the ___ (student) results were published online.’
questions.explanation: Plural noun ending in -s + apostrophe after the s.

questions.prompt: The city is proud of ___ long history.
questions.explanation: *its* = belonging to it; *it's* = it is.

questions.prompt: Which part is incorrect? *Unemployment fell sharply last year which surprised many economists.*
questions.explanation: A sentence-relative *which* clause needs a comma: *…last year, which surprised…*

questions.prompt: Which part is incorrect? *The three main causes are: poverty, poor housing and lack of education.*
questions.explanation: A colon must follow a complete clause; remove it after *are*.

questions.prompt: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence.
questions.explanation: Fronted subordinate clause → comma before the main clause.
options: If governments invest in public transport, car use tends to fall.
If governments invest in public transport car use, tends to fall.
If governments, invest in public transport car use tends to fall.
If governments invest, in public transport, car use tends to fall.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses commas to show that ALL the scientists were consulted?
questions.explanation: Commas make the clause non-defining: it adds information about all the scientists.
options: The scientists, who were consulted in advance, supported the plan.
The scientists who were consulted in advance supported the plan.
The scientists who, were consulted in advance supported the plan.
The scientists who were consulted, in advance supported the plan.

questions.prompt: Join with a semicolon and *therefore*. ‘The sample was small. The results should be treated with caution.’ → ‘The sample was small___ the results should be treated with caution.’
questions.explanation: Sentence adverb between two clauses: semicolon before, comma after.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is most appropriate in formal academic writing?
questions.explanation: Formal style avoids dashes, exclamation marks and contractions; *nevertheless* between clauses needs a semicolon.
options: The findings were unexpected; nevertheless, they were consistent with earlier studies.
The findings were unexpected – but they matched earlier studies!
The findings weren't expected, but they matched what others found.
The findings were unexpected, nevertheless they were consistent with earlier studies.

questions.prompt: Which sentence punctuates a list of complex items correctly?
